title: A 19-Year-Old Says He Found a Master Password in CBSE's Exam Grading System That Could Let Anyone Change Student Marks. CBSE Says It Was Just a Test Site.
excerpt: Nisarja Adhikari claims the On-Screen Marking portal's front-end code exposed a master password, broken OTP verification, and unauthenticated access to grading dashboards — CERT-In is investigating
body:
A 19-year-old amateur cybersecurity researcher says he found a master password sitting in plain view inside the code of CBSE's new digital exam-marking system — and that it could have allowed anyone to view and alter student grades. The Central Board of Secondary Education says the vulnerabilities existed only on a testing site and that the actual evaluation portal was never breached.

The truth, as usual, probably lies somewhere in the middle. But the controversy has exposed uncomfortable questions about how India's largest education board secures the marks of 3.4 million Class 12 students.

## What Nisarja Adhikari Found

Nisarja Adhikari, who completed his own Class 12 exams this year, published a detailed blog post on May 22 describing what he called "an absolute embarrassment" of security practices in CBSE's On-Screen Marking portal — the system introduced in February 2026 to digitize the evaluation of board exam answer sheets.

The OSM system works by scanning physical answer sheets and having examiners grade them through a web portal. CBSE says this reduces registration errors and manual involvement. Adhikari says the portal's security architecture treats that goal as optional.

His central finding: the Angular-based web application ships all of its front-end logic in a single JavaScript file that anyone can download, logged in or not. Inside that file, Adhikari claims he found an encrypted "master password" that bypasses the examiner login process entirely — no OTP, no two-factor authentication, just the password and a publicly available user ID and school code.

"With these, I was able to log in as an examiner, completely bypassing the OTP/2FA flow, and access the assessment dashboard where I could view and edit grades," Adhikari wrote.

## It Gets Worse

The master password was allegedly just the beginning. According to Adhikari's blog:

**The OTP system was broken by design.** When a user triggers authentication, the server sends the one-time password back in the response itself, and the browser compares it locally. "The secret you're supposed to prove you received is delivered directly to your browser, and the browser evaluates its own test," Adhikari wrote. A cybersecurity professional reviewing network requests would see the OTP in cleartext.

**Internal pages were accessible without authentication.** Dashboard, profile, evaluation views, and verification dashboards could allegedly be accessed by inserting fake values into browser storage and navigating directly to the URL.

**Password reset didn't verify the existing password.** Combined with what Adhikari described as a systemic IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) vulnerability, he claimed this could enable complete account takeover of examiner accounts — "without any credentials or inside access."

Adhikari says he reported the vulnerabilities to CERT-In, India's Computer Emergency Response Team, in February. A senior official from the Ministry of Electronics and IT confirmed to Hindustan Times that CERT-In was looking into the matter and had raised it with CBSE.

## CBSE's Response

The board pushed back firmly, saying the portal shown in Adhikari's screenshots — `cbse.onmark.co.in` — was a testing site with sample data, not the production system used for actual evaluation.

"The URL `http://cbse.onmark.co.in` is only the exam site with sample data for internal testing and review purposes," CBSE said in a post on X. "No security breach was identified in the OSM portal used in the actual evaluation process."

The distinction matters legally and technically. If Adhikari tested only a sandbox environment, the production portal may have entirely different security controls. But cybersecurity experts have noted that organizations frequently deploy testing environments using the same codebase as production — meaning the vulnerabilities Adhikari found could theoretically exist in both.

## The Larger Problem

India's education technology infrastructure is growing faster than its security practices. CBSE's OSM system handles evaluation for one of the world's largest board examination systems. The Aadhaar-linked digital identity ecosystem, the DigiLocker document platform, and the Academic Bank of Credits all handle sensitive student data at massive scale.

If a 19-year-old with a browser and curiosity can identify architectural flaws in a major exam system — whether testing or production — it raises the question of what a motivated actor with resources could do.

For the 3.4 million students who sat for CBSE Class 12 exams this year, the board's assurance that the production system is secure will need to be backed by something more convincing than a tweet. An independent security audit, publicly reported, would be a start.
author: Diaspora Desk
